pos: n. (the western Scottish see founded by Kentigern, raised to an archbishopric in 1492, and the chief city of the Scottish church's western province)
etymology: British glas cau, the green hollow, latinised Glasguensis; the burgh motto is Let Glasgow flourish by the preaching of the word.
biblical_def: Glasgow began as the church of Kentigern, called Mungo, who was bishop among the Britons of Strathclyde in the sixth century and was buried where the cathedral crypt now stands. The see was revived under David I about 1115, the cathedral built through the thirteenth century, a university founded in 1451, and the bishopric raised to an archbishopric in 1492 to balance St Andrews. At the Reformation the cathedral was saved from the hammer by the trade guilds of the town, which is why it is the only medieval cathedral on the Scottish mainland to survive entire. The burgh's motto in its full form is a sentence about means and not merely about prosperity: Glasgow is to flourish by the preaching of the word. The city afterwards became the capital of Scottish evangelical dissent, of the great mission societies, and of Chalmers's parish experiment in a manufacturing town. The dictionary records Glasgow for the motto, which states the right order. Commerce, learning and a cathedral are all effects; the cause is a word preached, and Acts measures the progress of the church by that word and by nothing else.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to preach as to pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject; to flourish as to thrive and prosper; a word as the sign of an idea, and the Scriptures; to grow as to increase in size; and fruit as that which is produced.
webster_full: PREACH, v.i. To pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject, or from a text of Scripture; to proclaim the gospel.
FLOURISH, v.i. To thrive; to grow luxuriantly; to be prosperous; to increase in wealth or honor.
WORD, n. An articulate sound used as the sign of an idea; in the plural, the Scriptures; also, the second person of the Trinity.
GROW, v.i. To increase in bulk or size by a natural, internal process; to advance; to improve.
FRUIT, n. Whatever is produced for the nourishment or gratification of man; the produce of any thing; effect or consequence.
corruption_summary: Western Scottish see of Kentigern, archbishopric from 1492, whose cathedral the trade guilds saved; its motto asks that the city flourish by the preaching of the word.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one in the motto: the church's growth is measured by the advance of a word and not by the size of the city. Luke writes the increase of the Ephesian church as a fact about the word itself, “So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed” (Act 19:20), and again of the Jerusalem church under persecution, “But the word of God grew and multiplied” (Act 12:24).

The live temptation is to shorten the motto, which the city has in fact done, so that flourishing is asked for without the means by which it was to come. Paul leaves no room for that abbreviation: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) is the whole commission, and the fruit follows the hearing rather than the hearing following the prosperity. Paul tells the Colossians that the gospel “bringeth forth fruit, as it doth also in you, since the day ye heard of it” (Col 1:6). A cathedral saved by guildsmen is a mercy; a word preached in it is the reason the mercy matters.

pos: n. (the Tayside burgh where the Scottish Reformation turned violent in 1559 and where the Five Articles were imposed in 1618)
etymology: British pert, a wood or copse; also called St Johnstoun from its church of St John the Baptist, whence the modern football name.
biblical_def: Perth sits on the Tay at the lowest bridging point, and for centuries it was where Scotland held its parliaments and assemblies. On 11 May 1559 John Knox preached in St John's and the congregation, after a priest began to prepare a mass, pulled down the images and then sacked the three friaries of the town; the regent brought an army, the Lords of the Congregation gathered, and the civil war that carried the Reformation had begun. In 1618 a General Assembly meeting in Perth was pressed by James VI into passing the Five Articles, which required kneeling at communion, private baptism, private communion for the sick, confirmation by bishops, and the observance of the five holy days; the kirk received them under protest and resented them for a generation. The dictionary records Perth because both of its famous episodes concern the limits of authority in the church. An assembly may bind consciences only where Christ has spoken, and its proper words are those of Jerusalem, that a thing seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to them, and that no greater burden was laid on the churches than the necessary things.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an assembly as a company met together; an image as a representation of any person or thing; to consider as to think on with care; a burden as that which is borne with labor; and necessary as that which must be.
webster_full: ASSEMBLY, n. A company or collection of individuals in the same place, usually for the same purpose; a congregation or ecclesiastical body met for worship or deliberation.
IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; an idol; a statue.
CONSIDER, v.t. To fix the mind on, with a view to a careful examination; to think on with care; to ponder; to study.
BURDEN, n. That which is borne or carried; a load; that which is grievous, wearisome or oppressive.
NECESSARY, a. That must be; that cannot be otherwise; indispensably requisite.
corruption_summary: Tayside burgh where Knox's 1559 sermon began the armed Reformation and where the 1618 Assembly was pressed into the Five Articles.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the rule of a church council, which is to decide by what God has spoken and to lay nothing else on the churches. Jerusalem met to deliberate, “And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6), and the decree that followed limited itself in terms no synod should ever exceed: it “seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things” (Act 15:28).

The two live temptations at Perth are opposite and both real. One is the mob's, which turns a right hatred of idols into general destruction; the commandment it appeals to is plain enough, “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4), and the Psalter's verdict on images is plainer, “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4) — yet neither text appoints a crowd to be the magistrate. The other temptation is the king's, which imposes ceremonies in the name of order and calls the result an assembly's decision. Perth saw both within sixty years.

pos: n. (the burgh at the mouth of the Ness, capital of the Highlands and the chief station of Gaelic preaching in the north)
etymology: Gaelic Inbhir Nis, the mouth of the Ness, from inbhir, a river mouth.
biblical_def: Inverness stands at the mouth of the Ness where the Great Glen meets the sea, and whoever held it held the road into the Highlands; Columba is said to have gone up the glen to it to meet the Pictish king Brude. Its importance to the church is linguistic. North and west of the town the people spoke Gaelic, and for two centuries after the Reformation the Lowland church had almost nothing in that tongue: the Irish Bible of Bedell and the Shorter Catechism in Gaelic had to serve until the Scottish Gaelic New Testament of 1767 and Bible of 1801. The Society in Scotland for Propagating Christian Knowledge planted schools from Inverness, at first teaching only English and so making children read a Bible they could not understand, until the policy was reversed. The Disruption of 1843 was followed in the Highlands more completely than anywhere else. The dictionary records Inverness for the plain apostolic rule about language in worship: Paul would rather speak five words with his understanding than ten thousand in a tongue the hearers do not know, and a church that forgets this is talking to the air.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tongue as a language; to understand as to have just ideas of; to teach as to instruct; to utter as to speak or pronounce; and air as the fluid we breathe, and figuratively, nothing.
webster_full: TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; a language; the whole sum of words used by a particular nation.
UNDERSTAND, v.t. To have just and adequate ideas of; to comprehend; to know the meaning of.
TEACH, v.t. To instruct; to inform; to communicate to another the knowledge of that of which he was before ignorant.
UTTER, v.t. To speak; to pronounce; to express; to disclose; to publish.
AIR, n. The fluid which we breathe; also, used of that which is empty, light or without substance.
corruption_summary: Highland capital at the mouth of the Ness, and the station from which the long struggle to preach and print in Gaelic was carried on.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that worship must be intelligible to the worshipper, which Paul settles by arithmetic: “I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue” (1Co 14:19). A Bible read in English to Gaelic children is the same error as a mass in Latin, however good the motive behind the schoolmaster's policy.

The second thing to name is the live temptation to treat a people's language as an obstacle to be removed rather than a vessel to be filled. Paul says what unintelligible speech actually accomplishes: “for ye shall speak into the air” (1Co 14:9). Pentecost ran the other way, and the wonder of it was precisely the mother tongue, “And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (Act 2:8). The remedy for a Highland parish was the one Paul prescribes for every parish, that the word of Christ should dwell in the people richly, “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16), which requires words they have.

pos: n. (the Perthshire see of Strathearn, whose bishop from 1661 was Robert Leighton)
etymology: Gaelic Dùn Bhlàthain, the fort of Blane, from the sixth-century missionary Blane of Bute.
biblical_def: Dunblane is a small cathedral town on the Allan Water, the see of the old diocese of Strathearn, named from Blane who worked among the southern Picts. Its cathedral was built in the thirteenth century under Bishop Clement, a Dominican, and the choir was kept in repair after the Reformation while the nave stood roofless for three hundred years. Its chief figure is Robert Leighton, made bishop there in 1661 at the Restoration and the one Scottish prelate of that era whom even the Covenanters found hard to hate: he refused to persecute, laboured at the accommodation schemes meant to bring presbyterians back without forcing episcopal orders on them, preached plainly, gave away his income, and resigned in disgust when the government preferred force. His commentary on the first epistle of Peter is still read. The dictionary records Dunblane for Leighton's example of what an overseer is. The office is a good work when a man desires the work and not the rank; the sin of his contemporaries was to take the title and leave the labour, and Peter forbids the thing by name when he tells the elders not to be lords over God's heritage.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bishop as an overseer; an office as a particular duty or charge; a pastor as a minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church; an ensample as a pattern; and heritage as inheritance or that which is possessed.
webster_full: BISHOP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent or ruler; in the primitive church, an elder or overseer of a particular church.
OFFICE, n. A particular duty, charge or trust conferred by public authority and for a public purpose; employment.
PASTOR, n. A shepherd; one that has the care of flocks and herds; a minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation.
ENSAMPLE, n. An example; a pattern or model for imitation.
HERITAGE, n. Inheritance; an estate that passes from an ancestor to an heir by descent; the people of God, as his possession.
corruption_summary: Perthshire see of Strathearn whose Restoration bishop, Robert Leighton, refused to persecute, laboured for accommodation, and resigned rather than coerce.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the oversight of a church is a labour before it is a dignity. Paul calls it a good work and makes the desire for the work, not the place, the test: “If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work” (1Ti 3:1), and the qualification he names is competence with the word, “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9).

The live temptation in Leighton's generation was to hold a see as a piece of royal patronage and enforce conformity with soldiers, and Peter forbids it in the plainest terms: elders are “Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3). What God promises his people is men of a particular kind rather than an office of a particular rank, “And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15). Leighton resigned because he could not feed a flock that was being driven.

pos: n. (the Angus see with an Irish round tower, a Culdee house turned cathedral chapter)
etymology: Probably from a Pictish personal name Brychan; the Gaelic is Breichin.
biblical_def: Brechin stands on the South Esk in Angus and keeps the only Irish round tower on the Scottish mainland apart from Abernethy, built about 1000 beside what was then a community of Culdees. The Culdees, the céli Dé or clients of God, were the surviving native clergy of the old Scottish church, living in small colleges and serving the people; at Brechin they were converted into the chapter of a new Latin cathedral in the twelfth century, and their name survived as a title long after their way of life had gone. The diocese was small and poor. At the Reformation its bishop, John Sinclair, married Mary to Darnley; afterwards it was a presbyterian stronghold, and in 1875 its cathedral was restored. The dictionary records Brechin for the Culdees, who are the clearest Scottish instance of a remnant: a body of native clergy, not learned, not powerful, keeping the services and the care of souls through centuries when the kingdom had almost no organised church at all. Scripture takes that pattern for granted and names it a work of grace, for a remnant is left not by its own strength but by election.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a remnant as that which remains after a part is removed; to leave as to suffer to remain; election as divine choice; to escape as to flee from danger; and to trust as to confide in.
webster_full: REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
LEAVE, v.t. To suffer to remain; to withdraw from and not take away; to permit to be or continue.
ELECTION, n. The choice of any person or thing; divine choice; predetermination of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy.
ESCAPE, v.i. To flee from and avoid; to be free or safe from danger; to avoid an evil.
TRUST, v.i. To confide; to rely; to depend with confidence on.
corruption_summary: Angus see with a round tower, whose Culdee community was absorbed into the cathedral chapter; the plainest Scottish instance of a surviving native clergy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of the remnant, which is a doctrine about God and not about the quality of the survivors. Isaiah says what Judah owed its continuance to: “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom” (Isa 1:9). Paul applies the same reckoning to his own day and names the cause exactly, “there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5).

The live temptation when the remnant is small is either to despise it as backward or to idealise it as pure. The Culdees were neither learned nor flawless, and they were what the Scottish church had. Isaiah promises their kind of return without flattering them, “The remnant shall return, even the remnant of Jacob, unto the mighty God” (Isa 10:21), and Zephaniah describes the material God works with in such periods: “I will also leave in the midst of thee an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD” (Zep 3:12). A poor chapter in a poor diocese kept the services going, which is the work of an afflicted and poor people.

pos: n. (the Angus abbey founded in 1178 by William the Lion, from which the Declaration of 1320 was sent to the pope)
etymology: Gaelic Aber Brothaig, the mouth of the Brothock burn; the older English form is Aberbrothock.
biblical_def: Arbroath Abbey was founded in 1178 by William the Lion for Tironensian monks from Kelso, and dedicated to Thomas Becket, whom the king had known in England. It grew rich on the Angus parishes and the North Sea trade, and its abbot sat in parliament. In April 1320 the barons of Scotland met there and sent to Pope John XXII the letter since called the Declaration of Arbroath, which argues that the Scots had their own ancient kingdom, that Bruce held it by the people's choice as well as by right, and that if he ever submitted it to England they would drive him out and take another king. It is the first clear European statement that a king rules on a condition. The abbey was ruined after the Reformation and quarried for the town. The dictionary records Arbroath because the Declaration's premise is scriptural whether its authors meant it so or not: crowns are given and removed by God, who changes the times and seasons and removes kings and sets up kings, and a nation is exalted by righteousness and not by its own antiquity.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a king as a chief ruler and sovereign; a kingdom as the territory subject to a king; righteousness as purity of heart and rectitude of life; a nation as a body of people inhabiting a country; and to exalt as to raise high.
webster_full: KING, n. The chief or sovereign of a nation; a man invested with supreme authority over a nation, tribe or country.
KINGDOM, n. The territory or country subject to a king; dominion; rule; sovereign power; also, the government of God.
RIGHTEOUSNESS, n. Purity of heart and rectitude of life; conformity of heart and life to the divine law.
NATION, n. A body of people inhabiting the same country, or united under the same sovereign or government.
EXALT, v.t. To raise high; to elevate; to elevate in power, wealth, rank or dignity.
corruption_summary: Angus abbey of 1178 where the barons of Scotland drew up the Declaration of Arbroath in 1320, the first clear European statement that a king rules conditionally.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the barons stumbled on, that no crown is held absolutely, because crowns are given. Daniel states it of the God who rules over empires: “he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Dan 2:21), and the watcher's decree declares the intent of such reversals, “to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men” (Dan 4:17).

The live temptation is nationalism, which takes the Declaration's argument about an ancient people and makes antiquity itself the title to God's favour. Scripture allows a nation its own bounds and history, and Paul grounds both in one decree: God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth” (Act 17:26). But the condition of a nation's standing is moral, not genealogical: “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34). A letter that limits a king is good; a creed that flatters a people is not.

pos: n. (the Perthshire Moot Hill where the kings of Scots were enthroned, and the Augustinian abbey burned in 1559)
etymology: Perhaps from Gaelic sgonn, a lump or mound, referring to the Moot Hill; the burgh spelling keeps the Scots pronunciation.
biblical_def: Scone, two miles above Perth on the Tay, is the place where the kings of Scots were made. The Moot Hill there held the Stone of Destiny until Edward I took it in 1296, and the enthronement at Scone, with the royal genealogy recited in Gaelic and the earls setting the king in the chair, was the act that made a king rather than a coronation by a bishop. Alexander I founded an Augustinian priory beside it about 1120, raised to an abbey, which kept the regalia and the records. In June 1559 the Reformation crowd from Perth came upstream and burned the abbey and the bishop's palace, against Knox's own attempts to restrain them. Charles II was crowned there in 1651, the last Scottish coronation. The dictionary records Scone for what an enthronement is and is not. A hill, a stone and a recited pedigree confer nothing; God is the judge who puts down one and sets up another, and the kingdom which is the LORD'S is not conveyed by any ceremony that men can perform or interrupt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a throne as a royal seat; a judge as one who presides in a court or decides a question; to set up as to erect or establish; a governor as one who rules; and to pluck up as to tear out by the roots.
webster_full: THRONE, n. A royal seat; a chair of state; the seat of a bishop; sovereign power and dignity.
JUDGE, n. A civil officer who is invested with authority to hear and determine causes; one who has skill to decide on any thing.
SET, v.t. To put or place; to fix; to establish; to appoint; to constitute, as to set up a king.
GOVERNOR, n. One who governs; one invested with supreme authority; a ruler; a director.
PLUCK, v.t. To pull with sudden force or effort; to pull off, out or up; to tear out by the roots.
corruption_summary: Perthshire Moot Hill where the kings of Scots were enthroned, with its Augustinian abbey, burned by the Reformation crowd in 1559.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that sovereignty is conferred by God and not by ceremony. The Psalmist sets the matter in a single line that leaves no office to the hill or the stone: “But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another” (Psa 75:7). Daniel says the same of the greatest empires, “he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Dan 2:21), so that the recited pedigree at Scone described a providence it could not create.

The live temptation at a national shrine is to believe that the rite makes the thing, and then to fight over the rite. The Stone was carried to Westminster, carried back, and argued over for seven centuries; the abbey that kept it was burned by Protestants in a fortnight of rioting. Through all of it the title stood where Scripture puts it: “For the kingdom is the LORD'S: and he is the governor among the nations” (Psa 22:28). The same God reserves the right to undo any realm he has made, “to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it” (Jer 18:7), which is a sobering word to read on a coronation hill.

pos: n. (the cathedral town of Caithness diocese in Sutherland, built by Bishop Gilbert de Moravia)
etymology: Gaelic Dòrnach, the place of fist-sized pebbles, from dòrn, a fist.
biblical_def: Dornoch is a small town on the Sutherland coast, the cathedral seat of the old diocese of Caithness, which covered the whole north of the mainland. Gilbert de Moravia, bishop from 1223, moved the see there after his predecessor Adam had been burned to death in his own kitchen at Halkirk by farmers enraged at his tithe demands; Gilbert built the cathedral, drew up a constitution for the chapter, and was the last Scot to be formally canonised before the Reformation. The cathedral was burned in a clan feud in 1570 and only partly restored until the nineteenth century. In 1727 Janet Horne was burned at Dornoch, the last judicial execution for witchcraft in Britain. The dictionary records Dornoch for the two deaths at either end of its story, a bishop killed over money and a confused old woman killed over superstition, and for the office that stands between such things and a people. A watchman is set to hear the word at God's mouth and warn them from him, and the whole use of the office is that the warning is God's and not the watchman's own.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a watchman as one who guards and gives warning; to warn as to give notice of danger; a tower as a lofty building for defence; safety as freedom from danger; and to reprove as to blame with kindness.
webster_full: WATCHMAN, n. A sentinel; a guard; one who is set to watch; one who keeps guard for the security of a city or camp.
WARN, v.t. To give notice of approaching or probable danger or evil; to caution against any thing that may prove injurious.
TOWER, n. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation and consisting of several stories; a fortress.
SAFETY, n. Freedom from danger or hazard; exemption from hurt, injury or loss.
REPROVE, v.t. To blame; to censure; to charge with a fault to the face; to chide; to reprehend.
corruption_summary: Sutherland cathedral town of the Caithness diocese; its bishop Adam was burned over tithes, Gilbert built the cathedral, and Britain's last witchcraft execution took place there in 1727.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the watchman's commission, which is not a licence to say what he thinks but an obligation to pass on what he has heard. Ezekiel has it in one sentence, with the source and the duty both named: “therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me” (Eze 33:7). The men who shouted from the wall in Isaiah are given no rest from the task, “which shall never hold their peace day nor night” (Isa 62:6).

The live temptation is the one Dornoch shows twice, a church using its office for revenue and a church lending its authority to a panic. Habakkuk stands his watch in the right posture, expecting correction as well as a message: “I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me” (Hab 2:1). And the refuge a watchman is to point to is never the institution he serves: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it” (Pro 18:10). Neither the tithe court nor the witch trial was that tower.

pos: n. (the Easter Ross burgh holding the shrine of Duthac, a chief Scottish pilgrimage resort of the later Middle Ages)
etymology: Probably from Norse thing, an assembly place; the Gaelic is Baile Dhubhthaich, Duthac's town.
biblical_def: Tain, on the Dornoch Firth in Easter Ross, grew round the relics of Duthac, an eleventh-century bishop whose bones were brought back from Ireland in 1253. Its collegiate church became the chief pilgrimage place of the north, and James IV came to it almost every year of his reign, sometimes on foot for part of the way, making offerings at the shrine; it was a sanctuary too, and the Earl of Ross's enemies were once dragged out of it and burned with the chapel. The shrine was swept away at the Reformation, and the burgh afterwards became a sober presbyterian market town. The dictionary records Tain as a clean example of what pilgrimage had become: a king on the road once a year to a box of bones, with an indulgence at the end of it. Scripture knows a pilgrimage of another kind altogether. Its pilgrims are men who confess that they have no settled place on the earth and who are looking for a city God has prepared; what they travel toward is future and promised, not a relic in a chapel in Ross.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pilgrim as a wanderer and a traveller to a holy place; a pilgrimage as a journey to a sacred place; a stranger as a foreigner; a country as a region or land; and a relic as the remains of a saint, kept with superstitious reverence.
webster_full: PILGRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveler; particularly, one who travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place, or to pay his devotion to the remains of dead saints.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A long journey, particularly a journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable, in order to pay devotion to the relics of some deceased saint.
STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one not an inhabitant; a guest.
COUNTRY, n. A region; a tract of land; the kingdom, state or territory in which one is born; the whole territory of a nation.
RELIC, n. That which remains; the remains of the body of a saint, or something belonging to a saint, kept with a superstitious reverence.
corruption_summary: Easter Ross burgh built round the shrine of Duthac, visited yearly by James IV and the chief pilgrimage resort of northern Scotland until the Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the scriptural sense of pilgrimage, which has no shrine in it at all. The writer to the Hebrews states the believer's position flatly: “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). The patriarchs are pilgrims in exactly that sense, having “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13) with no holy place to walk to.

The live temptation is to locate grace at a destination, which turns religion into travel and devotion into payment. The object the patriarchs desired was neither a relic nor a region, “But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city” (Heb 11:16). And the pilgrim's provision for the road is the word rather than a shrine at the end of it: “Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage” (Psa 119:54). James IV walked to Tain every year and died at Flodden; the statutes were available to him at home.

pos: n. (the Border abbey of Premonstratensian canons founded in 1150, burned three times by English armies)
etymology: Perhaps Old English drý burh, the dry fort, or from a British darach bruach, the oak bank; the canons' own charters write Dryburgum.
biblical_def: Dryburgh lies in a loop of the Tweed, the smallest and most sheltered of the four great Border abbeys, founded in 1150 by Hugh de Morville for white canons of the Premonstratensian order from Alnwick. Its position was its ruin: standing on the invasion road, it was burned by Edward II's army in 1322, by Richard II in 1385, and finally by the English in 1544 during the Rough Wooing, after which it was never rebuilt. The canons drifted away and the lands passed to laymen. The ruins became a romantic resort, and Walter Scott and Earl Haig are buried in the north transept. The dictionary records Dryburgh for what the Border abbeys teach about rebuilding. Three times the house went up again, and the fourth time it did not; and Scripture is far more interested in the repair of waste places than in the lament over them. The repairer of the breach is a title God gives to his people, and the promise attached to it is of foundations raised up for many generations, which outlasts any masonry on the Tweed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a breach as a gap or opening made by breaking; to repair as to restore to a sound state; waste as desolate ground; a foundation as the basis of a building; and distress as extreme anxiety or affliction.
webster_full: BREACH, n. The act of breaking, or state of being broken; a gap or opening made by breaking, as a breach in a wall.
REPAIR, v.t. To restore to a sound or good state after decay, injury, dilapidation or partial destruction; to refit; to mend.
WASTE, n. A desolate or uncultivated country; destruction; devastation; useless expense.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that part of a building which lies on the ground; the ground work of any thing.
DISTRESS, n. Extreme pain; anguish of body or mind; affliction; calamity; misery.
corruption_summary: Border abbey of white canons on the Tweed, founded 1150 and burned by English armies in 1322, 1385 and 1544, after which it stayed a ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God names his people after the work of rebuilding rather than after the grief of ruin. Isaiah gives the title and the promise in one verse: “they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations” (Isa 58:12). Amos has the same undertaking in the LORD'S own mouth, “In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen” (Amo 9:11).

The live temptation at a picturesque ruin is to prefer the ruin, to make a mood out of what was a disaster, and to bury celebrities in a transept where canons once sang. The Psalter does grieve properly over such things: “thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps” (Psa 79:1). But Nehemiah's response to an identical sight is not a poem; it is a building party: “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17). Dryburgh was rebuilt three times by men who thought that way.
